newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Most of Queensland Australia dry in April - govt.
newsitem.headline: Most of Queensland Australia dry in April - govt.

text.p: April rainfall in the Australian state of Queensland was generally confined to the coastal fringe, with most of the interior not receiving any productive rain, the state's Department of Primary Industries said in a bulletin.
Drier parts of the state experienced increasing rainfall deficits, it said.
The north region was very dry in April for most of the region except the wet tropical coast and some parts of the Atherton Tablelands, it said.

In the west region, very little effective rainfall was recorded. "Some areas which received limited rainfall during the wet season are beginning to exhibit early signs of a lean winter in terms of pasture availability," the department said.
Only scattered shower activity occurred in the central region during the month, it said.
In the southeast, April continued the run of variable rainfall totals with the weather generally dry.
Very little effective rainfall was recorded in the south region.

However, the majority of livestock and pasture areas of the north region received their best rainfall since 1991 and supplies of pasture and water were sufficient for the foreseeable future in most cases.
Pasture condition was still good to excellent in most areas, with stock in very good condition headed into winter, it said.
With virtually no useful rainfall in the west, pasture had hayed off considerably with protein levels dropping in many areas.
Pasture was abundant in the central region but was rapidly starting to hay off.
This followed widespread rainfall over much of the region.
In the southeast, pasture availability varied greatly with the condition of most stock generally being maintained.
Low stock numbers and short high quality feed had helped maintain condition but this would be changed in the short-term with the onset of frosts, it said.
In the south, rainfall ensured that feed supplies were adequate for stock in most areas except the Darling Downs.
On crops, most of the south region's sorghum had been harvested, with good yields recorded, it said.
In cotton, dryland yields and quality were mixed because of a dry spell in the January and early February period and were also affected in some areas by insect attack, it said.
The soil moisture profile in many areas remained adequate for winter planting but further rainfall would be needed soon to ensure a large winter planting, it said.

Climate forecasts suggest that the chance of average rainfall during the May-July period is now about 30 percent for some areas of Queensland and 65 percent in the southeast corner of the state, it said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
